standards.name: Observations Data Model 2 (ODM2)
standards.abstract: ODM2 is an information model and supporting software ecosystem for spatially-discrete, feature-based Earth observations. It is designed to represent observations arising from field and laboratory activities (Actions) and their Results, supporting many data modalities including time series, measurements, profiles, and spectra. ODM2 was developed by the ODM2 community (drawing on ODM1, PetDB/SedDB, and OGC Observations & Measurements) and is maintained via the ODM2 GitHub organization; it supplies relational schema scripts, controlled vocabularies, best-practice guidance, and software (APIs, loaders, web apps, YODA file format) to enable consistent capture, sharing, and service-oriented publication of environmental observation data.

classification.rationale: The source material is the ODM2 information model and documentation that defines concrete entities and named attributes (e.g., Results: ResultUUID, ResultType, VariableID, UnitsID, ResultDateTime, etc.), describes controlled vocabularies and data types, and provides blank relational schema scripts - i.e., explicit field-level structure rather than only prose guidance or a workflow. The documentation lists table-like fields and their expected types/constraints, so this is a genuine metadata TABLE-style standard.

standards.name: OGC Observations & Measurements (O&M) / ISO 19156
standards.abstract: The source XML is an example ObservationCollection encoding water temperature measurements from a buoy (platform 014). Observations include sampling time (ISO8601), geolocation (latitude/longitude), depth, and observed property values (water temperature in degC), encoded in an SWE DataArray within O&M. OGC Observations & Measurements (O&M), also standardized as ISO 19156, is an interoperability model and XML/GML/SWE encoding maintained by the Open Geospatial Consortium (and formalized by ISO) that defines how to represent observations, sampling times, procedures (sensors), features of interest, observed properties, result structures and encodings. The standard addresses the problem of consistent representation and exchange of sensor and observation data across systems and covers the conceptual model (observations, sampling, FOI, procedure) and common encodings such as SWE DataArray and DataRecord for results.

classification.rationale: The source material provides a concrete data-structure encoding (an SWE DataArray/DataRecord) with named swe:field elements each having a clear name and data type/encoding (e.g. Time, Quantity with uom), which corresponds to a table-like schema of data columns.

standards.name: YODA (YAML Observation Data Archive & exchange) File Format
standards.abstract: YODA is a YAML-based metadata and data packaging format for observational environmental and specimen data (time series, specimen measurements, tabular datasets). The examples and parser files show records for datasets, people/authors, spatial references, sampling features/sites, methods, variables/units, processing levels, actions/feature-actions, results and time-series result values; data are recorded as YAML mappings and arrays and often reference controlled vocabularies (CV) and ODM2 fields. The material is from the YODA-Tools repository (examples and parser code) and provides concrete YAML templates and example instances illustrating the file structure, required sections, and field names that the format uses for exchanging observational and specimen data.

classification.rationale: The source material is a machine-oriented YAML schema and many example YAML files that present explicit named fields (DataSetUUID, DataSetTypeCV, PersonFirstName, SamplingFeatureUUID, etc.) with concrete expected values/types (UUIDs, floats, datetimes, controlled vocabulary codes). This is field-level metadata structure (a metadata table / schema), not a prose checklist or a procedural DAG.

standards.name: SKOS / RDF exposure for controlled vocabularies
standards.abstract: This document describes how controlled vocabularies (CVs) are managed and exposed for the ODM2 project. The CVs are used to validate vocabulary terms inside an ODM2 database (CV tables in the CV extension) and are made available via a web registry (vocabulary.odm2.org) with support for viewing terms, requesting changes, and programmatic access. To improve interoperability, the vocabularies are exposed via a RESTful API that returns RDF/XML using SKOS encoding; individual vocabularies and terms have stable URLs. The material is authored by the ODM2 project as guidance on hosting, moderation, and machine-accessible exposure of its controlled vocabularies.

classification.rationale: The source is descriptive prose explaining policies and mechanisms for hosting and exposing controlled vocabularies; it does not present a structured metadata table of fields/types nor a sequence of ordered steps. The content is best represented as principles/instructions and factual statements about the CV system rather than as a DAG or table.

principles.principle: Validate vocabulary terms against CV tables within the ODM2 database.
principles.evidence: the validity of vocabulary terms will be assessed internally within an ODM2 database against a listing found in a CV table corresponding to each vocabulary.

principles.principle: CV tables are organized within the ODM2 CV extension.
principles.evidence: CV tables are found within the [CV extension](http://odm2.github.io/ODM2/schemas/ODM2_Current/diagrams/ODM2CV.html).

principles.principle: Provide a public repository and registry where users can view vocabularies and request changes.
principles.evidence: So, we decided that we needed an initial repository and registry where ODM2 users could access the existing CV terms, request modifications to existing terms, and suggest new terms.

principles.principle: Host the ODM2 controlled vocabularies at a dedicated website (vocabulary.odm2.org).
principles.evidence: ODM2 CVs are currently hosted at: http://vocabulary.odm2.org

principles.principle: Offer human-facing pages to list vocabularies, list terms, show term details, and accept change requests.
principles.evidence: At this website, you can view the list of vocabularies, view the terms in each vocabulary, and view the details of each individual term. Change requests for either new terms or modifications to existing terms can also be made on this website.

principles.principle: Assign stable, individual URLs to each vocabulary and each term.
principles.evidence: all vocabularies and terms are accessible via individual URLs (e.g., http://vocabulary.odm2.org/actiontype/ to access the ActionTypeCV and http://vocabulary.odm2.org/actiontype/observation/ to access the descrption of an individual term.

principles.principle: Expose vocabularies via a RESTful API that returns RDF/XML using SKOS encoding to improve interoperability.
principles.evidence: they have been exposed in RDF/XML format via a RESTful API using Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS) encoding.

principles.principle: Provide example API endpoints that return SKOS RDF/XML for vocabularies and for individual terms.

http://vocabulary.odm2.org/api/v1/actiontype/observation/?format=skos - Returns an RDF/XML document containing an individual term within the ActionTypeCV

principles.principle: Consider external registries (e.g., MMI ORR) but maintain a moderation system appropriate to the community's needs.
principles.evidence:
MMI ORR includes convenient vocabulary and vocabulary mapping management capabilities, and ontology and vocabulary term URI resolvers that are both user (human) and machine friendly.

However, MMI doesn't yet offer the community vocabulary moderation system we wanted initially for ODM2 (especially in support of the Critical Zone Observatory Information Managers).
